content: 1. Children and adolescents presenting with symptoms and signs suggestive of tuberculosis (TB) should be evaluated using treatment decision algorithms. If treatment is indicated, it should be initiated promptly. Specimen collection should be performed using less invasive methods whenever feasible, or patients should be referred to appropriate facilities for further evaluation. 2. All children and adolescents receiving TB treatment or tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT) must be registered with the district National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) office to ensure proper monitoring and follow-up. 3. Contact investigation for TB should be conducted to identify children and adolescents who either exhibit symptoms and signs of TB or are asymptomatic but eligible for TPT. Those with symptoms should be managed according to national guidelines, including referral to higher levels of care if necessary. 4. Source cases of TB should be identified, and close contacts of children or adolescents diagnosed with TB should be screened for the disease. 5. Follow-up care must be arranged for children and adolescents undergoing TB treatment or TPT to ensure adherence and monitor progress. 6. Sick children and adolescents, particularly those with danger signs, should be referred to the first referral level of care as per national guidelines. Non-responders to TB treatment should also be referred for further evaluation. 7. Patientand family-centered care should be prioritized, including nutritional support, counseling on the disease, adherence to treatment, and completion of therapy. Support systems should be in place to assist families throughout the treatment process. 8. Comprehensive TB health education should be provided, covering infection prevention, potential side effects of TB medications, and appropriate actions to take in case of adverse events. 9. HIV counseling and testing should be offered to all children and adolescents with TB, and follow-up care for HIV-related needs should be arranged. 10. Adolescents require special attention to ensure confidentiality, access to adolescent-friendly services, and opportunities for support. 11. Collaboration with schools is essential to enhance TB contact investigation and treatment support. Educating teachers and staff about TB can reduce stigma and minimize disruptions to education for affected children and adolescents. 12. Health care facilities providing TB services should have access to diagnostic supplies and child-friendly formulations of TB medications. Referral systems for sample analysis should be established if on-site diagnostic tools are unavailable. 13. Decentralization of TB services requires investment in infrastructure, capacity-building for health care providers, and community engagement. Over time, these costs are expected to decrease as services become more integrated and efficient. 14. Integrated TB services should be planned to bring care closer to where children, adolescents, and families live. This includes mapping health care delivery points and assessing the needs of facilities to implement TB services effectively. 15. TB disproportionately affects individuals of lower socioeconomic status, exacerbating poverty and social deprivation. The disease often leads to catastrophic costs for families, including medical expenses, lost income, and educational disruptions for children. 16. Family-centered models of care should be developed to mitigate the socioeconomic impact of TB on children and adolescents. This includes strategies to reduce direct and indirect costs while ensuring treatment adherence and completion. 17. Social protection measures are critical for children and adolescents with TB, addressing issues such as food insecurity, education, and financial stability. Multisectoral collaboration is necessary to provide comprehensive TB care. 18. Training and support for health care workers at the primary level are essential to build confidence and capacity in diagnosing and managing pediatric TB. Task-shifting to trained lay health workers can also enhance service delivery. 19. Lessons from country experiences highlight the feasibility of implementing decentralized, family-centered, and integrated TB services across various health care levels. These approaches have been effective in improving TB case detection and management in children and adolescents.
